Margaret Ellery Vaughn (1912–1998) was an American botanist and conservationist whose long-term studies of coastal salt marshes shaped the modern understanding of tidal wetlands. She grew up on her family's farm near Ipswich, Massachusetts, the eldest of four children, and spent most of her childhood outdoors, pressing flowers and recording the seasons in a notebook her father had given her. After completing a degree in botany at Mount Holyoke College she joined the state agricultural station, where she spent twelve years mapping the distribution of marsh grasses and recording how the vegetation shifted with the tides. Her field notes from this period, later donated to the college archive, remain a standard source for ecologists working along the eastern seaboard.

Colleagues remembered Vaughn as a patient and exacting observer who disliked laboratory work and preferred to spend whole days wading through mud with a notebook in one hand and a measuring stick in the other. She argued, against the prevailing view of her teachers, that salt marshes were not transient landscapes destined to fill in and disappear but stable communities maintained by the daily rhythm of the tides. That argument, developed over decades of quadrat surveys, eventually became the accepted account of how these systems persist.

Her most widely cited paper, a survey of seagrass and marsh vegetation across thirty-two estuaries, was published in 1957 in the journal Ecological Monographs. The paper described how the same handful of species arranged themselves differently depending on how sheltered a creek mouth happened to be, and it introduced a simple scheme for classifying marsh zones that other researchers were still using half a century later. Reviewers praised the clarity of the writing and the sheer volume of data, which represented more than twenty thousand separate observations collected by hand.

Vaughn also wrote for a general audience. Her short book on the natural history of the salt marsh, illustrated with her own ink drawings, sold modestly but was reprinted twice and is still recommended to visitors at several wildlife refuges. She corresponded widely with amateur naturalists, answered every letter she received, and kept a running list of the species reported to her from places she had never visited, a list she called her borrowed marsh.

In her later years Vaughn campaigned against the drainage and development of tidal wetlands, testifying at public hearings and writing to local newspapers. She was not a gifted speaker, and she disliked the confrontations that public meetings involved, but she was persistent, and several of the protections she argued for were eventually written into state law. Her colleagues sometimes complained that she spent too much time on correspondence and too little on publishing, though most of them conceded that her letters were often more useful than many of the papers they read.

She died at her home in Ipswich after a long illness, survived by two daughters and a wide circle of former students. A small scholarship for field botanists was established in her memory, and a stretch of protected marshland near the town was later named for her. Her papers are held by the college library.
